claim: Public health emergencies like SARS, MERS, and COVID-19 have prioritized surveillance of zoonotic coronaviruses.
source: Public health emergencies like SARS, MERS, and COVID-19 have prioritized surveillance of zoonotic coronaviruses, resulting in extensive genomic characterization of coronavirus diversity in bats.
evidence: This is a statement about the impact of public health emergencies on surveillance priorities, supported by established knowledge of pandemic responses.

claim: Most bat coronaviruses have been characterized solely by PCR amplification of small regions from the best-conserved gene.
source: Sequencing viral genomes directly from animal specimens remains a laboratory challenge, however, and most bat coronaviruses have been characterized solely by PCR amplification of small regions from the best-conserved gene.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations throughout the manuscript (e.g., Drexler et al., 2014; Geldenhuys et al., 2021) and is a characterization of the state of the field.

claim: A custom panel of 20,000 probes was used to capture and sequence coronavirus genomic material in 21 swab specimens collected from bats in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
source: Using a custom panel of 20,000 probes, we captured and sequenced coronavirus genomic material in 21 swab specimens collected from bats in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental design and methods used in the study.

claim: For 15 of 21 specimens, probe capture recovered more genome sequence than had been previously generated with standard amplicon sequencing protocols.
source: For 15 of these specimens, probe capture recovered more genome sequence than had been previously generated with standard amplicon sequencing protocols, providing a median 6.1-fold improvement (ranging up to 69.1-fold).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing probe capture to amplicon sequencing results.

claim: Probe capture provided a median 6.1-fold improvement in genome recovery compared to amplicon sequencing, ranging up to 69.1-fold.
source: For 15 of these specimens, probe capture recovered more genome sequence than had been previously generated with standard amplicon sequencing protocols, providing a median 6.1-fold improvement (ranging up to 69.1-fold).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the comparison of probe capture and amplicon sequencing methods.

claim: Probe capture data identified five novel alpha- and betacoronaviruses in the specimens.
source: Probe capture data also identified five novel alpha- and betacoronaviruses in these specimens, and their full genomes were recovered with additional deep sequencing.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the discovery results from the study.

claim: Full genomes of five novel coronaviruses were recovered with additional deep sequencing.
source: Probe capture data also identified five novel alpha- and betacoronaviruses in these specimens, and their full genomes were recovered with additional deep sequencing.
evidence: This describes the outcome of deep sequencing performed on selected specimens.

claim: Four endemic human coronaviruses have been identified as common causes of mild respiratory illnesses since the 1960s.
source: Since the 1960s, four endemic human CoVs have been identified as common causes of mild respiratory illnesses (Corman et al., 2018; Ye et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and SARS-CoV-2 have caused severe disease, public health emergencies, and global crises in the past two decades.
source: In the past two decades, additional CoV threats have emerged, most notably SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and SARS-CoV-2, causing severe disease, public health emergencies, and global crises (Drosten et al., 2003; Zaki et al., 2012; Hu et al., 2015; Corman et al., 2018; Ye et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and represents established knowledge about recent coronavirus outbreaks.

claim: Coronavirus spill-overs have established CoVs alongside influenza A viruses as important zoonotic pathogens and pandemic threats.
source: These spill-overs have established CoVs alongside influenza A viruses as important zoonotic pathogens and pandemic threats.
evidence: This is an inference based on the impact of recent coronavirus pandemics and established knowledge in the field.

claim: Some historical pandemics may have been mis-attributed to influenza and may have in fact been spill-overs of now-endemic human coronaviruses.
source: Indeed, evolving perceptions of CoV risk have led to speculation that some historical pandemics have been mis-attributed to influenza, and they may have in fact been the spill-overs of now-endemic human CoVs (Vijgen et al., 2005; Corman et al., 2018; Brüssow and Brüssow, 2021).
evidence: This is explicitly described as speculation and is supported by citations.

claim: Bats are the second-most diverse order of mammals, following rodents.
source: They are the second-most diverse order of mammals, following rodents, and they are a vast reservoir of CoV diversity (Drexler et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2015; Frutos et al., 2021; Geldenhuys et al., 2021; Ruiz-Aravena et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a factual statement about bat diversity supported by citations.

claim: Bats are a vast reservoir of coronavirus diversity.
source: They are the second-most diverse order of mammals, following rodents, and they are a vast reservoir of CoV diversity (Drexler et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2015; Frutos et al., 2021; Geldenhuys et al., 2021; Ruiz-Aravena et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Bats have been implicated in the emergence of SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2, and the endemic human coronaviruses NL63 and 229E.
source: Bats have been implicated in the emergence of SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2, and, less recently, the endemic human CoVs NL63 and 229E (Li et al., 2005; Pfefferle et al., 2009; Tong et al., 2009; Huynh et al., 2012; Corman et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2015; Tao et al., 2017; Ye et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2020; Ruiz-Aravena et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to published literature.

claim: Recovering viral genomes directly from animal specimens remains a laboratory challenge.
source: Genomic sequencing has been instrumental for characterizing CoV diversity and potential zoonotic threats, but recovering viral genomes directly from animal specimens remains a laboratory challenge.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of laboratory methods, supported by knowledge in the field.

claim: Host tissues and microbiota contribute excessive background genomic material to specimens, diluting viral genome fragments.
source: Host tissues and microbiota contribute excessive background genomic material to specimens, diluting viral genome fragments and vastly increasing the sequencing depth required for target detection and accurate genotyping.
evidence: This is an explanation of why recovering viral genomes is challenging, based on established knowledge of specimen composition.

claim: Laboratory methods for targeted enrichment of viral genome material have been necessary for practical, high-throughput sequencing of surveillance specimens.
source: Consequently, laboratory methods for targeted enrichment of viral genome material have been necessary for practical, high-throughput sequencing of surveillance specimens (Houldcroft et al., 2017; Fitzpatrick et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents established practice in the field.

claim: Amplicon sequencing uses PCR to amplify target genomic material.
source: The first, called amplicon sequencing, uses PCR to amplify target genomic material.
evidence: This is a definition of amplicon sequencing based on established knowledge.

claim: Amplicon sequencing is comparatively straightforward and sensitive.
source: It is comparatively straightforward and sensitive, but PCR chemistry limits amplicon length and relies on the presence of specific primer sites across diverse taxa (Houldcroft et al., 2017; Fitzpatrick et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a characterization of amplicon sequencing supported by citations.

claim: PCR chemistry limits amplicon length and relies on the presence of specific primer sites across diverse taxa.
source: It is comparatively straightforward and sensitive, but PCR chemistry limits amplicon length and relies on the presence of specific primer sites across diverse taxa (Houldcroft et al., 2017; Fitzpatrick et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes limitations of PCR-based methods, supported by citations.

claim: Extensive genomic divergence within viral taxa often constrains amplicon locations to the most conserved genes, limiting phylogenetic resolution.
source: In practice, extensive genomic divergence within viral taxa often constrains amplicon locations to the most conserved genes, limiting phylogenetic resolution (Drexler et al., 2014; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations and describes a practical limitation of amplicon sequencing.

claim: Studies of coronavirus diversity have been almost exclusively based on small regions of the relatively conserved RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) gene.
source: Due to these limitations, studies of CoV diversity have been almost exclusively based on small regions of the relatively conserved RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) gene (Drexler et al., 2014; Geldenhuys et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a characterization of the state of coronavirus diversity studies, supported by citations.

claim: Hybridization probe capture uses longer nucleotide oligomers to anneal and immobilize complementary target genomic fragments while background material is washed away.
source: The second major paradigm for enriching viral genomic material is called hybridization probe capture. This method uses longer nucleotide oligomers to anneal and immobilize complementary target genomic fragments while background material is washed away.
evidence: This is a description of the probe capture method based on established knowledge.

claim: Probes are typically 80–120 nucleotides in length.
source: Probes are typically 80–120 nucleotides in length, making them more tolerant of sequence divergence and nucleotide mismatches than PCR primers (Brown et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a technical specification supported by citation.

claim: Probes are more tolerant of sequence divergence and nucleotide mismatches than PCR primers.
source: Probes are typically 80–120 nucleotides in length, making them more tolerant of sequence divergence and nucleotide mismatches than PCR primers (Brown et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a comparative statement about probe characteristics supported by citation.

claim: Probe panels are highly scalable, allowing for the simultaneous capture of thousands to millions of target sequences.
source: Probe panels are also highly scalable, allowing for the simultaneous capture of thousands to millions of target sequences.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of probe panels based on established knowledge.

claim: Probe capture has been popular for applications where diverse and hypervariable viruses are targeted.
source: This has made them popular for applications where diverse and hypervariable viruses are targeted (Bonsall et al., 2015; Briese et al., 2015; O'Flaherty et al., 2018; Wylezich et al., 2021; Wylie et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Probe capture has only been occasionally used to attempt sequencing of bat coronaviruses.
source: Probe capture has only been occasionally used to attempt sequencing of bat CoVs, however (Lim et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a characterization of the literature supported by citations.

claim: 4,852 bat coronavirus genomic sequences were obtained from GenBank for probe design.
source: We obtained 4,852 bat CoV genomic sequences from GenBank, used them to design a custom panel of 20,000 probe sequences, then assessed in silico how extensively these reference sequences were covered by our custom panel (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data collection for probe design.

claim: For 90% of bat coronavirus sequences, the custom panel covered at least 94.32% of nucleotide positions.
source: For 90% of these bat CoV sequences, the custom panel covered at least 94.32% of nucleotide positions.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from in silico analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: For 90% of full-length bat coronavirus genomes, the custom panel covered at least 98.73% of nucleotide positions.
source: We also evaluated probe coverage for the subset of these sequences representing full-length bat CoV genomes (Figure 1B), and 90% of these targets had at least 98.73% of their nucleotide positions covered.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from in silico analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The custom probe panel provided broad coverage of known bat coronavirus diversity at the time the panel was designed.
source: These results showed broad probe coverage of known bat CoV diversity at the time the panel was designed.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in silico coverage analysis.

claim: 25 metagenomic sequencing libraries were prepared from 21 bat oral and rectal swabs collected in DRC between 2015 and 2018.
source: We used our custom panel to assess probe capture recovery of CoV material in 25 metagenomic sequencing libraries. We prepared these libraries from a retrospective collection of 21 bat oral and rectal swabs that had been collected in DRC between 2015 and 2018 (Kumakamba et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the experimental materials used in the study.

claim: The swabs were collected as part of the PREDICT project, a large-scale USAID Emerging Pandemic Threats initiative that has collected over 20,000 animal specimens from 20 coronavirus hotspot countries.
source: These swabs had been collected as part of the PREDICT project, a large-scale United States Agency for International Development (USAID) Emerging Pandemic Threats initiative that has collected over 20,000 animal specimens from 20 CoV hotspot countries (e.g. Anthony et al., 2017; Lacroix et al., 2017; Nziza et al., 2020; Valitutto et al., 2020; Ntumvi et al., 2022).
evidence: This provides context about the specimen collection program, supported by citations.

claim: Coronaviruses had been previously detected in these specimens with PCR assays by Quan et al., 2010, and Watanabe et al., 2010.
source: CoVs had been previously detected in these specimens with PCR assays by Quan et al., 2010, and Watanabe et al., 2010.
evidence: This describes prior work on these specimens, supported by citations.

claim: Sanger sequencing of amplicons by Kumakamba et al., 2021, had generated partial RdRp sequences of 286 or 387 nucleotides.
source: Sanger sequencing of these amplicons by Kumakamba et al., 2021, had generated partial RdRp sequences of 286 or 387 nucleotides, which had been used to assign these specimens to four novel phylogenetic groups of alpha- and betacoronaviruses (Table 1).
evidence: This describes prior characterization of the specimens, supported by citation.

claim: Partial RdRp sequences were used to assign specimens to four novel phylogenetic groups of alpha- and betacoronaviruses.
source: Sanger sequencing of these amplicons by Kumakamba et al., 2021, had generated partial RdRp sequences of 286 or 387 nucleotides, which had been used to assign these specimens to four novel phylogenetic groups of alpha- and betacoronaviruses (Table 1).
evidence: This describes the phylogenetic classification from prior work, supported by citation.

claim: 113 coronavirus contigs were recovered from 17 of 25 libraries.
source: In total, 113 CoV contigs were recovered from 17 of 25 libraries.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the de novo assembly analysis.

claim: The median contig size with probe capture for specimens processed with the Watanabe et al. protocol was 696 nucleotides.
source: The protocol by Watanabe et al. had generated 387 nucleotide-long partial RdRp sequences, but median contig size with probe capture for these specimens was 696 nucleotides (IQR: 453–1051 nucleotides, max: 19,601 nucleotides).
evidence: This is a quantitative result comparing probe capture to amplicon sequencing.

claim: The median contig size with probe capture for specimens processed with the Quan et al. protocol was 602 nucleotides.
source: The protocol by Quan et al. had generated 286 nucleotide-long partial RdRp sequences, but median contig size with probe capture for these specimens was 602 nucleotides (IQR: 423–1053 nucleotides, max: 4240 nucleotides).
evidence: This is a quantitative result comparing probe capture to amplicon sequencing.

claim: 107 contigs (93.8%) were longer than the partial RdRp sequence previously generated for their specimen by standard amplicon sequencing protocols.
source: Overall, 107 contigs (93.8%) were longer than the partial RdRp sequence previously generated for their specimen by standard amplicon sequencing protocols, demonstrating the capacity of probe capture to recover larger contiguous fragments of CoV genome sequence.
evidence: This is a quantitative result demonstrating the advantage of probe capture.

claim: Nucleotide identities between probe capture contigs and partial RdRp amplicon sequences ranged from 99.3% to 100%.
source: We also assessed nucleotide sequence concordance; for specimens where the partial RdRp amplicon sequence was successfully assembled, nucleotide identities ranged from 99.3% to 100% (median = 100%, maximum two mismatches).
evidence: This is a quantitative result assessing sequence accuracy.

claim: The median total assembly size was 1724 nucleotides.
source: The median total assembly size was 1724 nucleotides (IQR: 0–5834 nucleotides), while median assembly N50 size was 533 nucleotides (IQR: 0–908 nucleotides) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from assembly analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The median assembly N50 size was 533 nucleotides.
source: The median total assembly size was 1724 nucleotides (IQR: 0–5834 nucleotides), while median assembly N50 size was 533 nucleotides (IQR: 0–908 nucleotides) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from assembly analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The median breadth of reference sequence recovery for all libraries was 2376 nucleotides.
source: The median breadth of reference sequence recovery for all libraries was 2376 nucleotides (IQR: 306–9446 nucleotides).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from reference-based mapping analysis.

claim: Phylogenetic group Q-Alpha-4 had a median reference sequence recovery of 6497 nucleotides.
source: Most libraries (48%) represented specimens from phylogenetic group Q-Alpha-4, which had a median reference sequence recovery of 6497 nucleotides (IQR: 733–9802 nucleotides, max: 12,673 nucleotides).
evidence: This is a quantitative result for a specific phylogenetic group.

claim: Phylogenetic group W-Beta-3 provided the libraries with the most extensive reference sequence recoveries, with a maximum of 26,755 nucleotides.
source: Phylogenetic group W-Beta-3 also accounted for a substantial fraction of libraries (32%), and although median reference sequence recovery was lower than for Q-Alpha-4 (2427 nucleotides), W-Beta-3 provided the libraries with the most extensive reference sequence recoveries (IQR: 780–19,286 nucleotides, max: 26,755 nucleotides).
evidence: This is a quantitative result for a specific phylogenetic group.

claim: The median ratio of probe capture recovery to amplicon sequencing recovery was 6.1-fold, reaching a maximum of 69.1-fold.
source: The median ratio was 6.1-fold (IQR: 0.8-fold to 33.0-fold), reaching a maximum of 69.1-fold.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of the two methods.

claim: Probe capture recovery was greater for 18 of 25 libraries (72%), representing 15 of 21 specimens (71%).
source: Probe capture recovery was greater for 18 of 25 libraries (72%), representing 15 of 21 specimens (71%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result comparing the success rate of probe capture.

claim: RdRp was more completely recovered than spike gene.
source: Overall, RdRp was more completely recovered than spike.
evidence: This is a comparative observation from the gene coverage analysis.

claim: No complete spike genes were recovered by probe capture.
source: No complete spike genes were recovered.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a negative result from the study.

claim: No coronavirus sequences were recovered from 4 of 25 libraries (representing three specimens).
source: No CoV sequences were recovered from 4 of 25 libraries (representing three specimens), despite partial RdRp sequences being obtained from them previously.
evidence: This is a statement of a negative result from the study.

claim: All partial RdRp amplicons had at least 95.3% of their nucleotide positions covered by the probe panel.
source: All partial RdRp amplicons had at least 95.3% of their nucleotide positions covered by the probe panel (Figure 5A), but this did not translate into extensive recovery.
evidence: This is a result from in silico probe coverage analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: For 12 of 25 libraries, no part of the partial RdRp sequence was recovered.
source: For 12 of 25 libraries, no part of the partial RdRp sequence was recovered, and full/nearly full recovery (>95%) of the partial RdRp sequence was achieved for only 7 of 25 libraries (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result about recovery success shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Full or nearly full recovery (>95%) of the partial RdRp sequence was achieved for only 7 of 25 libraries.
source: For 12 of 25 libraries, no part of the partial RdRp sequence was recovered, and full/nearly full recovery (>95%) of the partial RdRp sequence was achieved for only 7 of 25 libraries (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a quantitative result about recovery success shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Median RNA integrity number (RIN) values for specimens were 1.1.
source: Median RNA integrity number (RIN) values and RNA concentrations for these specimens were low: 1.1 and 14 ng/μl respectively, as was expected from archived material (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of specimen quality shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Median RNA concentrations for specimens were 14 ng/μl.
source: Median RNA integrity number (RIN) values and RNA concentrations for these specimens were low: 1.1 and 14 ng/μl respectively, as was expected from archived material (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement of specimen quality shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The relationship between RNA concentration and genome recovery was significant (p=0.045, Spearman's rank correlation).
source: This relationship was significant for RNA concentration (p=0.045, Spearman's rank correlation), but not for RNA integrity despite trending towards significance (p=0.053, Spearman's rank correlation).
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis.

claim: The relationship between RNA integrity and genome recovery was not significant (p=0.053, Spearman's rank correlation).
source: This relationship was significant for RNA concentration (p=0.045, Spearman's rank correlation), but not for RNA integrity despite trending towards significance (p=0.053, Spearman's rank correlation).
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis.

claim: The median abundance of viral material was 0.26 million genome copies/μl.
source: The median abundance of viral material was 0.26 million genome copies/μl.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from RT-qPCR measurements.

claim: There was a strong and significant monotonic relationship between viral abundance and extent of genome recovery (p<0.0001, Spearman's rank correlation).
source: There was a strong and significant monotonic relationship between viral abundance and extent of genome recovery (p<0.0001, Spearman's rank correlation).
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis.

claim: Probe coverage was nearly complete for all reference sequences.
source: Probe coverage was nearly complete for all reference sequences (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a result from in silico probe coverage analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Reference sequence recovery did not exceed 92.3% for any library.
source: Nonetheless, reference sequence recovery did not exceed 92.3% for any of these libraries, and complete spike genes were conspicuously absent (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative result about the maximum recovery achieved.

claim: The results indicated the presence of coronaviruses with novel spike genes that diverged from the spike genes of reference sequences and all other coronaviruses described in GenBank.
source: These results indicated the presence of CoVs similar to bat CoV CMR704-P12 and Chaerephon bat corornavirus/Kenya/KY22/2006, except with novel spike genes that diverged from the spike genes of these reference sequences and all other CoVs described in GenBank.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of genome recovery.

claim: Complete genomes were recovered from five specimens: CDAB0017RSV, CDAB0040RSV, CDAB0203R, CDAB0217R, and CDAB0492R.
source: Complete genomes were only recovered from five specimens: CDAB0017RSV, CDAB0040RSV, CDAB0203R, CDAB0217R, and CDAB0492R.
evidence: This is a direct statement of which specimens yielded complete genomes.

claim: On-target rates for deep metagenomic sequencing ranged from 0.003% to 0.064%.
source: On-target rates, that is, the percentage of total reads mapping to the CoV genome, were calculated (Figure 7A). These ranged from 0.003% to 0.064%, revealing the extremely low abundance of viral genomic material present in these swabs.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from mapping analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Low prevalence of viral genomic material is one challenging characteristic of swab specimens.
source: Considering these were the most successful libraries, these results highlighted that low prevalence of viral genomic material is one challenging characteristic of swab specimens.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the low on-target rates observed.

claim: On-target rates for captured libraries ranged from 11.3% to 45.1% of valid reads.
source: On-target rates for captured libraries ranged from 11.3% to 45.1% of valid reads (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from mapping analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: A 1020-fold difference was observed between mean on-target rates for deep-sequenced unenriched metagenomic libraries (0.029%) and probe captured libraries (29.6%).
source: Instead, we compared mean on-target rates for the deep-sequenced unenriched metagenomic libraries (0.029% mean on-target) against the original probe captured libraries (29.6% mean on-target); we observed a 1020-fold difference between these means, with the probe captured on-target rates significantly higher (p<0.001, t-test on two independent means).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from statistical comparison of enrichment.

claim: Probe captured on-target rates were significantly higher than unenriched libraries (p<0.001, t-test on two independent means).
source: Instead, we compared mean on-target rates for the deep-sequenced unenriched metagenomic libraries (0.029% mean on-target) against the original probe captured libraries (29.6% mean on-target); we observed a 1020-fold difference between these means, with the probe captured on-target rates significantly higher (p<0.001, t-test on two independent means).
evidence: This is a statistical result confirming enrichment effectiveness.

claim: Novel spike protein sequences from specimens CDAB0017RSV and CDAB0040RSV formed a monophyletic clade.
source: Spike protein sequences from specimens CDAB0017RSV and CDAB0040RSV formed a monophyletic clade, as did those from specimens CDAB0203R and CDAB0217R, reflecting their membership in partial RdRp-based phylogenetic groups W-Beta-2 and W-Beta-3, respectively (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Novel spike protein sequences from specimens CDAB0203R and CDAB0217R formed a monophyletic clade.
source: Spike protein sequences from specimens CDAB0017RSV and CDAB0040RSV formed a monophyletic clade, as did those from specimens CDAB0203R and CDAB0217R, reflecting their membership in partial RdRp-based phylogenetic groups W-Beta-2 and W-Beta-3, respectively (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Novel spike proteins grouped with spike protein sequences from three betacoronaviruses in GenBank: HQ728482.1, MG693168.1, and NC_048212.1.
source: These novel spike proteins also grouped with spike protein sequences from three betacoronaviruses in GenBank: HQ728482.1, MG693168.1, and NC_048212.1 (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: The spike protein sequence from specimen CDAB0492R grouped with spikes from two alphacoronaviruses in GenBank: HQ728486.1 and MZ081383.1.
source: The spike protein sequence from specimen CDAB0492R, the lone Q-Alpha-4 representative, grouped with spikes from two alphacoronaviruses in GenBank: HQ728486.1 and MZ081383.1 (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 9.

claim: None of the coronaviruses recovered from these specimens were closely related to coronaviruses that infect humans based on spike gene homology.
source: None of the CoVs recovered from these specimens were closely related to CoVs that infect humans based on spike gene homology.
evidence: This is a conclusion from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Pairwise global alignments of spike amino acid sequences were all less than 76.5% identical and less than 85.7% positive.
source: Alignments completely covered all novel spike sequences, but they were all less than 76.5% identical and less than 85.7% positive (Table 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sequence alignment analysis shown in Table 3.

claim: Only specimens CDAB0203R and CDAB0217R were collected from the same bat species as their closest spike protein matches in GenBank (Eidolon helvum).
source: Only specimens CDAB0203R and CDAB0217R were collected from the same bat species as their closest spike protein matches in GenBank (Eidolon helvum).
evidence: This is a comparative observation from metadata analysis.

claim: All study specimens were collected from the DRC, but their closest GenBank matches were collected from diverse locales, including neighbouring Kenya, Cameroon in West Africa, and Yunnan province in China.
source: All study specimens were collected from the DRC, but their closest GenBank matches were collected from diverse locales, including neighbouring Kenya, Cameroon in West Africa, and Yunnan province in China.
evidence: This is a comparative observation from metadata analysis.

claim: Low alignment scores, disparate host species, and dispersed collection locations suggest these viruses belong to extensive but hitherto poorly characterized taxa of coronavirus.
source: Taken together, these low alignment scores, disparate host species, and dispersed collection locations suggested these viruses belong to extensive but hitherto poorly characterized taxa of CoV.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: For specimen CDAB0017RSV, sequence similarity to the closest GenBank match was so low that no alignment was generated for the spike gene.
source: For specimen CDAB0017RSV, sequence similarity was so low that no alignment was generated for the spike gene (Table 4).
evidence: This is a result from nucleotide alignment analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: Nucleotide alignments for spike genes were all incomplete (18–83% coverage) with low nucleotide identities (71.5–84.6%).
source: Nucleotide alignments for the other specimens were all incomplete (18–83% coverage of the novel spike sequence) with low nucleotide identities (71.5–84.6%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from nucleotide alignment analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: Probe capture can achieve more extensive genome recovery from surveillance specimens than standard amplicon sequencing protocols.
source: This study highlights the potential for probe capture to recover greater extents of CoV genome compared to standard amplicon sequencing methods.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative results of the study.

claim: Recovering more extensive fragments from diverse regions of the genome would provide additional genetic sequence to compare against reference sequences in databases like GenBank and RefSeq.
source: Recovering more extensive fragments from diverse regions of the genome would also provide additional genetic sequence to compare against reference sequences in databases like GenBank and RefSeq.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the benefits of more extensive genome recovery.

claim: Sequences from additional genome regions could be used to identify coronaviruses where recombination has occurred.
source: Sequences from additional genome regions could also be used to identify CoVs where recombination has occurred, which is increasing recognized as a potential hallmark of zoonotic CoVs (Hu et al., 2015; Corman et al., 2018; Ye et al., 2020; Ruiz-Aravena et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents a potential application of the method.

claim: Recombination is increasingly recognized as a potential hallmark of zoonotic coronaviruses.
source: Sequences from additional genome regions could also be used to identify CoVs where recombination has occurred, which is increasing recognized as a potential hallmark of zoonotic CoVs (Hu et al., 2015; Corman et al., 2018; Ye et al., 2020; Ruiz-Aravena et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Failure to capture complete spike gene sequences, even from libraries with otherwise extensive coverage, was successfully used to predict the presence of novel spike genes.
source: In this study, failure to capture complete spike gene sequences, even from libraries with otherwise extensive coverage, was successfully used to predict the presence of novel spike genes.
evidence: This describes how negative results provided useful information.

claim: Contiguity across recovered regions can be used to evaluate abundance and intactness of viral genomic material, identifying specimens where deep metagenomic sequencing is likeliest to succeed.
source: Furthermore, contiguity across recovered regions can be used to evaluate abundance and intactness of viral genomic material, identifying specimens where deep metagenomic sequencing is likeliest to succeed.
evidence: This is an inference about how probe capture results can guide downstream decisions.

claim: In vitro sensitivity appeared to be the most limiting factor for probe capture in this study.
source: The first, which appeared to be the most limiting in this study, is the in vitro sensitivity of this method.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of factors affecting recovery.

claim: Probe capture must be performed on already constructed metagenomic sequencing libraries.
source: Probe capture must be performed on already constructed metagenomic sequencing libraries.
evidence: This is a statement about the technical requirements of the method based on established knowledge.

claim: The library construction process involves numerous sequential biochemical reactions and bead clean-ups, where inefficiencies result in compounding losses of input material.
source: The library construction process involves numerous sequential biochemical reactions and bead clean-ups, where inefficiencies result in compounding losses of input material.
